Anatomy & Physiology.q: A clinician mistakenly records that the periodontal ligament is a hard tissue. What is incorrect about this statement?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The periodontal ligament is a fibrous connective tissue, not a hard tissue.

n.0: It is not mineralised.
n.2: It has a blood supply.
n.3: It is not enamel.
n.4: It is not dentine.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient presents with inflammation of the tissue surrounding the teeth within the oral cavity. Which structure is most likely affected?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The gingiva (gums) surround the teeth and are commonly affected by inflammation such as gingivitis.

n.0: The hard palate forms the roof of the mouth, not surrounding teeth.
n.2: The tongue is involved in taste and movement, not surrounding teeth.
n.3: Buccal mucosa lines the cheeks, not directly surrounding teeth.
n.4: The soft palate is located posteriorly in the roof of the mouth.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dentist asks the nurse to retract the patient's tongue to examine the structure that connects it to the floor of the mouth. What is the best action?

n.0: The uvula is located at the soft palate.
n.2: The soft palate is posterior and not under the tongue.
n.3: Gingiva is around the teeth, not under the tongue.
n.4: Buccal mucosa is in the cheeks.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient presents with plaque accumulation primarily on the inner surfaces of their lower incisors. Which tooth surface is most affected?

n.0: The labial surface is the outer surface facing the lips.
n.2: Occlusal surfaces are found on posterior teeth, not incisors.
n.3: Mesial refers to the surface toward the midline, not the inner surface.
n.4: Distal refers to the surface away from the midline.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient complains of sensitivity when brushing the outer surface of their front teeth. Which surface is most likely affected?

n.0: Lingual surfaces face the tongue.
n.2: Mesial surfaces are between teeth.
n.3: Distal surfaces are away from the midline.
n.4: Occlusal surfaces are not present on anterior teeth.

n.3: Buccal and occlusal surfaces are not proximal contact areas.

n.3: Cementum protects the root but is not involved in pulp inflammation.
n.4: The periodontal ligament supports the tooth but is not the central tissue affected.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A clinician observes wear facets on the chewing surfaces of posterior teeth. What is the correct term for these surfaces?

n.3: Mesial surfaces are toward the midline.
n.4: Distal surfaces are away from the midline.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient presents with gingivitis. Which structure is primarily inflamed?

n.0: Enamel is not inflamed.

n.3: Pulp inflammation is pulpitis.
n.4: Bone inflammation is not gingivitis.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: Which oral cavity structure is primarily responsible for housing taste buds and aiding in speech and mastication?

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is assisting during a restoration of a molar where the chewing surface is being treated. Which surface is the dentist working on?

Anatomy & Physiology.q: Which surface of an anterior tooth is primarily involved when a patient chips the biting edge of an incisor?

Anatomy & Physiology.q: Which salivary gland contributes the greatest proportion of resting saliva in the oral cavity?

Anatomy & Physiology.q: During an oral examination, a structure is identified as forming the anterior roof of the mouth and consisting of bone. What is this structure?

Cross Infection & Decontamination.q: A member of staff places a used matrix band into a domestic bin. What is the main concern?
Cross Infection & Decontamination.w: Potentially contaminated clinical items should be placed in the correct designated waste stream.

n.0: Weight is not the main issue.
n.2: Colour matters only insofar as correct segregation; wrong stream is the issue.
n.3: Noise is irrelevant.
n.4: Space is secondary.

Cross Infection & Decontamination.q: What is the main reason for dating sterilised packs?
Cross Infection & Decontamination.w: Dating packs supports stock rotation and helps identify items needing review or reprocessing.

n.0: Dating is not cosmetic.
n.2: Weight is irrelevant.
n.3: Dating does not reduce documentation needs.
n.4: Cycle time is unaffected.

Cross Infection & Decontamination.q: Using the image, which feature best indicates intended segregation of contaminated and sterile items?
Cross Infection & Decontamination.w: Clearly labelled zones support workflow separation between contaminated and sterilised instruments.

n.0: Glove colour does not define workflow segregation.
n.2: Sharps bin size does not indicate zoning.
n.3: Tap type is not the main segregation control shown.
n.4: Hand rub placement alone does not define clean and dirty zones.

Cross Infection & Decontamination.q: Which identification best describes why packs are sealed before storage?
Cross Infection & Decontamination.w: Sealed packs maintain a protective barrier until point of use.

n.0: Sealing is not for cosmetic appearance.
n.2: Weight is irrelevant.
n.3: Packaging does not reduce documentation needs.
n.4: Appointment length is unrelated.

Cross Infection & Decontamination.q: Which item is most suitable for routine labelling after sterilisation?
Cross Infection & Decontamination.w: Cycle date and batch details support stock rotation and traceability.

n.0: Patient names are not routine pack labels for stock items.
n.1: Irrelevant information does not aid traceability.
n.3: Room colour has no decontamination value.
n.4: Chair number alone is insufficient traceability.

Cross Infection & Decontamination.q: Using the image, which feature most helps staff recognise correct workflow direction?
Cross Infection & Decontamination.w: Clearly marked dirty and clean bench labels guide correct movement of instruments through the area.

n.0: Dispenser height does not define workflow direction.
n.2: Waste bin colours may assist waste segregation but not overall flow.
n.3: Sink size does not indicate movement routes.
n.4: Goggle position is not the key workflow control shown.

Cross Infection & Decontamination.q: A dental nurse notices that a clinician has removed gloves after treatment but keeps the same mask on while preparing instruments for decontamination. What is the main risk in this scenario?
o: Cross-contamination from a contaminated mask surface
Cross Infection & Decontamination.w: Masks may become contaminated during treatment and should not be handled or worn into clean decontamination tasks unnecessarily.

n.1: Fogging may occur but is not the principal infection-control risk here.
n.2: Glove powder is unrelated to the mask being reused.
n.3: Transport timing is secondary to contamination risk.
n.4: Noise is irrelevant to PPE safety.

Cross Infection & Decontamination.q: What is the main purpose of keeping dirty zones physically separate from clean zones?
Cross Infection & Decontamination.w: Physical separation helps prevent microorganisms transferring from contaminated to clean items or surfaces.

n.0: Paperwork reduction is unrelated.
n.2: Space may help workflow but is not the main purpose.
n.3: Décor is irrelevant.
n.4: Break times are unrelated.

Cross Infection & Decontamination.q: What is the main purpose of waste segregation in a dental practice?
Cross Infection & Decontamination.w: Waste segregation supports safety, legal compliance and correct downstream disposal.

n.0: Lighting costs are unrelated.
n.2: Appointment times are unrelated.
n.3: Décor is irrelevant.
n.4: Waste segregation does not store instruments.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient with suspected anaphylaxis is deteriorating rapidly. Which item from the emergency kit is most likely to be required urgently?
Medical Emergencies.w: Adrenaline is a key emergency drug used in suspected anaphylaxis according to training and local protocols.

n.1: Articulating paper is a dental consumable, not an emergency medicine.
n.2: Fluoride varnish has no role in acute anaphylaxis management.
n.3: Impression materials are unrelated to emergency treatment.
n.4: Temporary filling materials are not used for medical emergencies.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient becomes pale and briefly loses consciousness after standing quickly from the chair, then rapidly recovers when laid flat. What is the most likely recognition?
Medical Emergencies.w: Brief loss of consciousness with quick recovery after lying flat is typical of syncope.

n.1: Stroke deficits usually persist rather than resolve immediately on lying flat.
n.2: Cardiac arrest would not rapidly self-resolve with normal recovery.
n.3: Anaphylaxis would usually include allergic symptoms.
n.4: Asthma primarily causes respiratory symptoms.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient suddenly develops unilateral facial droop, slurred speech and weakness in one arm in the dental chair. What emergency should be recognised?
Medical Emergencies.w: Facial droop, arm weakness and speech disturbance are classic stroke warning signs.

n.1: Hypoglycaemia can mimic some symptoms but focal FAST signs strongly suggest stroke.
n.2: Syncope usually causes faintness or loss of consciousness rather than one-sided weakness.
n.3: Asthma causes breathing difficulty rather than focal neurological deficit.
n.4: Panic attacks do not typically cause unilateral weakness.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient collapses in reception, is unresponsive and not breathing normally. CPR has started and the AED has just arrived. What is the best immediate action regarding AED use?
o: Switch on the AED and apply the pads without delaying compressions unnecessarily
Wait until two full minutes of CPR are completed before turning on the AED
Check the patient’s pulse again before deciding whether to use the AED
Move the patient into the surgery before attaching the AED pads
Provide oxygen first and use the AED only if there is no improvement
Medical Emergencies.w: The AED should be turned on promptly and pads applied as soon as available while minimising interruptions to CPR.

n.1: Defibrillation should not be delayed unnecessarily once an AED is available.
n.2: Repeated pulse checks delay treatment and are not the priority.
n.3: Moving the patient first may waste critical time unless safety requires it.
n.4: Oxygen does not replace urgent AED use in suspected cardiac arrest.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient becomes pale, sweaty and says they feel faint while seated upright in the dental chair. What is the best immediate management?
o: Lay the chair back, raise the legs and monitor the patient
Ask the patient to walk to reception for fresh air
Give oral glucose immediately without assessment
Continue treatment quickly to finish the procedure
Sit the patient further upright and observe
Medical Emergencies.w: Suspected syncope is managed by positioning the patient flat with legs elevated to improve cerebral perfusion.

n.1: Walking may worsen fainting and increase risk of collapse.
n.2: Glucose is not first-line unless hypoglycaemia is suspected.
n.3: Treatment should stop while the emergency is managed.
n.4: Upright positioning may worsen reduced blood flow to the brain.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally. What sequence should follow first?
o: Call for help, start CPR, send for the AED
Check blood pressure, then look for an AED
Move the patient to reception, then assess breathing
Give two drinks of water, then reassess
Wait one minute to see if recovery occurs
Medical Emergencies.w: Immediate priorities are summoning help, starting CPR and retrieving the AED.

n.1: Blood pressure checks delay life-saving treatment.
n.2: Unnecessary movement delays CPR.
n.3: Water is inappropriate for an unresponsive patient.
n.4: Waiting wastes critical time.

Medical Emergencies.q: While assessing breathing, a collapsed patient has occasional gasping sounds. How should this be interpreted?
o: Agonal breathing and treat as not breathing normally
Adequate breathing if the chest rises sometimes
A sign that CPR should be delayed
Medical Emergencies.w: Occasional gasps are agonal respirations and should not be mistaken for normal breathing.

n.1: Agonal gasps are abnormal and often occur in cardiac arrest.
n.2: Hyperventilation presents differently and the patient is collapsed.
n.3: Intermittent gasps do not indicate effective breathing.
n.4: CPR should not be delayed when agonal breathing is present.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient becomes drowsy, very thirsty and reports frequent urination over the last day. Breath smells fruity. Which interpretation is most accurate?
o: This may indicate hyperglycaemia requiring urgent medical assessment
This is straightforward hypoglycaemia needing oral glucose only
This is a mild asthma flare-up
This is syncope due to anxiety
Medical Emergencies.w: Thirst, polyuria, drowsiness and fruity breath suggest significant hyperglycaemia or ketoacidosis.

n.1: Hypoglycaemia usually causes sweating, tremor and rapid onset symptoms.
n.2: Asthma does not explain thirst and fruity breath.
n.3: Syncope is usually sudden and transient.
n.4: These signs are not typical post-seizure features alone.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient has central chest pain not relieved by their own GTN spray and looks clammy. What is the best management?
o: Call emergency services and manage as possible myocardial infarction
Continue treatment but shorten the appointment
Ask the patient to drive home and rest
Place them in the recovery position immediately
Medical Emergencies.w: Persistent chest pain with systemic symptoms may indicate myocardial infarction and requires urgent escalation.

n.1: Continuing treatment delays urgent care.
n.2: Glucose does not treat suspected cardiac chest pain.
n.3: The patient should not self-transport in this situation.
n.4: Recovery position is not first-line for a conscious chest pain patient.

Medical Emergencies.q: During treatment, a patient suddenly becomes pale, sweaty and says they feel faint after seeing the local anaesthetic needle. What is the most likely emergency being recognised?
Medical Emergencies.w: Pallor, sweating and feeling faint triggered by anxiety are classic features of vasovagal syncope.

n.1: Asthma usually presents with wheeze, breathlessness and chest tightness.
n.2: Seizure would more commonly involve altered consciousness or convulsive activity.
n.3: Hyperglycaemia develops more gradually and commonly causes thirst or lethargy.
n.4: Anaphylaxis often includes airway, breathing or skin changes after exposure.

Medical Emergencies.q: Which item is most appropriate basic equipment to assist ventilation during a medical emergency?
Medical Emergencies.w: A pocket mask is designed to help deliver rescue breaths more safely during resuscitation.

n.1: An impression tray is not used for ventilation.
n.2: A cheek retractor does not provide assisted ventilation.
n.3: An endodontic ruler is unrelated to airway support.
n.4: A wax knife has no emergency airway function.

Medical Emergencies.q: An AED advises a shock. What is the best action immediately before pressing the shock button?
o: Ensure nobody is touching the patient
Remove both pads and dry the chest again
Medical Emergencies.w: Before shock delivery, everyone must be clear of contact with the patient for safety and effective shock administration.

n.1: Do not delay a prompted shock to give breaths.
n.2: If a shock is advised, it should be delivered promptly.
n.3: Pads should remain in place unless incorrectly attached.
n.4: A prolonged pulse check delays defibrillation.

Medical Emergencies.q: The AED announces, 'No shock advised.' The patient remains unresponsive and not breathing normally. What is the best action?
o: Resume CPR immediately until the AED re-analyses or the patient recovers
Turn the AED off because it is no longer needed
Check blood pressure before deciding what to do next
Remove the pads and place the patient in recovery position
Wait without touching the patient for ten minutes
Medical Emergencies.w: If no shock is advised and the patient remains in cardiac arrest, CPR should continue immediately.

n.1: The AED should remain attached for ongoing guidance.
n.2: Blood pressure checks are not the priority during arrest.
n.3: Recovery position is only for breathing unconscious patients.
n.4: Doing nothing would be unsafe and delays CPR.

Medical Emergencies.q: During AED analysis, a team member continues chest compressions. How should this be interpreted?
o: This may interfere with rhythm analysis and should stop when prompted
This improves accuracy by keeping circulation moving
This is required whenever only one rescuer is present
This prevents the AED from advising an unnecessary shock
This is acceptable if compressions are shallow
Medical Emergencies.w: Movement during analysis can interfere with rhythm detection, so compressions should stop when the AED instructs.

n.1: Although compressions are important, they should pause briefly for analysis when prompted.
n.2: Single-rescuer CPR still follows AED voice prompts.
n.3: Continuing movement can reduce analysis accuracy, not improve it.
n.4: Compression depth is unrelated to the need to pause for analysis.

Medical Emergencies.q: A diabetic patient becomes shaky, confused and sweaty while waiting for treatment after missing lunch. What is the most likely emergency?
Medical Emergencies.w: Sweating, tremor and confusion in a diabetic who has missed food strongly suggest hypoglycaemia.

n.1: Hyperventilation causes rapid breathing and tingling rather than low glucose symptoms.
n.2: Hyperglycaemia is typically slower in onset and less associated with sweating.
n.3: TIA causes focal neurological symptoms rather than typical low glucose signs.
n.4: MI may cause chest pain or collapse rather than classic low glucose presentation.

Medical Emergencies.q: The AED says, 'Shock advised.' What is the most appropriate action immediately before pressing the shock button?
o: Ensure everyone is clear and nobody is touching the patient
Give two rescue breaths to improve oxygenation first
Check for signs of circulation for 30 seconds
Remove one pad briefly and reapply it
Continue compressions while the shock is delivered
Medical Emergencies.w: Before shock delivery, all rescuers must be clear of the patient to avoid harm and allow safe defibrillation.

n.1: Breaths should not delay a shock once advised.
n.2: A prolonged circulation check delays defibrillation.
n.3: Pads should stay attached unless incorrectly placed.
n.4: No one should touch the patient during shock delivery.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient develops wheeze and increasing breathlessness during treatment. They have their reliever inhaler with them. What is the best immediate management?
o: Help the patient use their reliever inhaler and sit upright
Lay the patient flat and continue treatment
Give oral glucose because they are distressed
Ask them to breathe into a paper bag
Place them in the recovery position
Medical Emergencies.w: For an asthma attack, assist with reliever inhaler use and position comfortably upright.

n.1: Lying flat may worsen breathing difficulty.
n.2: Glucose does not treat bronchospasm.
n.3: Paper bag breathing is inappropriate and unsafe.
n.4: Recovery position is not for a conscious breathless patient.

Medical Emergencies.q: Which finding most strongly identifies that CPR should be started immediately on an adult patient?
o: Drowsy with a weak radial pulse
Medical Emergencies.w: CPR is indicated when the patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally after assessment.

n.1: This may indicate illness but does not by itself indicate cardiac arrest.
n.2: The patient is breathing and requires urgent assessment, not immediate CPR.
n.3: Presence of circulation signs means cardiac arrest is not confirmed.
n.4: This suggests possible postural hypotension or other causes, not arrest.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient has chest pain, becomes grey, clammy and increasingly short of breath. Which sequence of recognition priorities is best?
o: Recognise possible acute coronary syndrome and worsening circulation
Recognise mild indigestion then continue treatment
Medical Emergencies.w: Chest pain with pallor, clamminess and breathlessness suggests serious cardiac compromise.

n.1: Serious causes must be considered first, not indigestion.
n.2: Needle phobia does not explain progressive chest symptoms.
n.3: Muscle strain is less likely with systemic deterioration.
n.4: Postural dizziness does not fit persistent chest pain and breathlessness.

Medical Emergencies.q: While attaching AED pads, a colleague places one pad directly over a visible medication patch on the chest. What error should be corrected?
o: Remove or avoid the patch area and place the pad on clean dry skin
Leave the patch in place because it improves adhesion
Place the second pad over the same patch for balance
Delay pad placement until the patient regains consciousness
Use only one pad if a patch is present
Medical Emergencies.w: Pads should not be placed over medication patches. The patch should be removed or avoided according to training, then pads applied to dry skin.

n.1: Patches may interfere with contact and create risk.
n.2: Both pads should not be placed over the same area.
n.3: Defibrillation should not be delayed unnecessarily.
n.4: AEDs require two pads unless device-specific instructions state otherwise.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient collapses in the surgery. After confirming unresponsiveness and calling for help, what sequence should follow?
o: Open airway, assess breathing, start compressions if not breathing normally
Check blood pressure, give oxygen, then assess airway
Move patient to wheelchair, then assess breathing
Give rescue breaths first, then check responsiveness
Medical Emergencies.w: After calling for help, airway and breathing are assessed promptly; if breathing is absent or abnormal, CPR begins.

n.1: Blood pressure measurement delays life-saving assessment.
n.2: Moving the patient unnecessarily delays treatment.
n.3: Breathing assessment should not be skipped.
n.4: Responsiveness is checked before deciding on CPR.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient is lying on a wet floor after collapse. CPR is in progress and the AED is ready. What is the best action?
o: Move or dry the patient away from pooled water before shock delivery if it can be done quickly
Ignore the wet floor because AED shocks are insulated
Delay all treatment until maintenance staff arrive
Apply the pads but never use the shock function
Stand in the water while pressing the shock button
Medical Emergencies.w: Water presents a hazard. The patient should be moved or the area dried promptly if feasible, while maintaining resuscitation efforts.

n.1: Environmental hazards should not be ignored.
n.2: Treatment should continue with sensible risk management, not full delay.
n.3: If a shock is advised, it may be needed once the environment is made safer.
n.4: Rescuers should avoid contact with water during shock delivery.

Medical Emergencies.q: A conscious diabetic patient becomes sweaty, shaky and confused. Which basic emergency item is most appropriate to prepare first?
Medical Emergencies.w: Likely hypoglycaemia in a conscious patient is commonly managed initially with a fast-acting glucose source if safe to swallow.

n.1: Rubber dam equipment is unrelated to low blood glucose treatment.
n.2: A matrix band is restorative equipment, not emergency equipment.
n.3: Etching gel is not used in medical emergencies.
n.4: A mouth mirror has no therapeutic role here.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient becomes unresponsive with tonic-clonic limb movements and jaw clenching. What emergency is most likely being recognised?
Medical Emergencies.w: Loss of consciousness with tonic-clonic movements is typical of a generalised seizure.

n.1: Syncope may involve brief twitching but not sustained tonic-clonic activity typically.
n.2: Stroke may reduce consciousness but convulsive presentation is less typical here.
n.3: Anaphylaxis primarily affects airway, breathing and circulation.
n.4: Angina causes chest pain rather than convulsions.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient develops facial swelling, wheeze and feels faint after exposure to latex. What is the best action?
o: Treat as anaphylaxis and administer adrenaline if trained and available
Offer water and observe for ten minutes
Ask the patient to walk outside for air
Continue treatment because symptoms may settle
Medical Emergencies.w: Airway, breathing and circulatory symptoms after exposure suggest anaphylaxis requiring urgent treatment.

n.1: Observation alone is unsafe in suspected anaphylaxis.
n.2: Walking may worsen collapse risk.
n.3: Dental treatment must stop during an emergency.
n.4: GTN does not treat allergic reactions.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient collapses and is unresponsive with abnormal breathing. Which equipment should be brought immediately if available?
Medical Emergencies.w: For suspected cardiac arrest, an AED should be retrieved urgently alongside CPR measures.

n.1: A shade guide is unrelated to emergency resuscitation.
n.2: An amalgam carrier is not emergency equipment.
n.3: X-ray accessories do not help manage cardiac arrest.
n.4: A periodontal probe has no role in immediate resuscitation.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient with stroke symptoms is conscious and breathing normally. Which management approach is most appropriate?
o: Call emergency services promptly and monitor airway and responsiveness
Give them oral glucose routinely before assessment
Lay them fully flat and leave them alone
Ask them to walk to the car for hospital transfer
Medical Emergencies.w: Suspected stroke requires urgent emergency referral with close monitoring.

n.1: Glucose is not routinely given without indication.
n.2: Leaving the patient unattended is unsafe.
n.3: Treatment should cease immediately.
n.4: The patient should not self-mobilise or self-transport.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient recovers after a fainting episode. Which sequence is most appropriate before discharge?
o: Reassess fully, allow gradual sitting up, confirm recovery, then decide on discharge
Stand them up immediately and escort them out
Restart treatment before asking how they feel
Leave them alone in the surgery to rest
Medical Emergencies.w: Patients recovering from syncope should be reassessed and returned upright gradually once stable.

n.1: Sudden standing may trigger recurrence.
n.2: Treatment restart should only follow full recovery and review.
n.3: Adrenaline is not routine for syncope.
n.4: Patients should continue to be observed.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient with a history of angina develops central chest pressure during treatment that improves after using their GTN spray. Which condition is most likely recognised?
Medical Emergencies.w: Chest discomfort relieved by GTN in a patient with known angina is consistent with an angina episode.

n.1: Cardiac arrest presents with collapse and absent normal responsiveness.
n.2: Hypoglycaemia usually causes sweating, confusion or behavioural change.
n.3: Seizure presents differently with abnormal movements or altered awareness.
n.4: Stroke commonly causes focal neurological deficits rather than GTN-responsive chest pain.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient is breathing rapidly, has tingling fingers, dizziness and appears very anxious after treatment starts. What is the most likely emergency being recognised?
Medical Emergencies.w: Rapid breathing with tingling and anxiety is consistent with hyperventilation.

n.1: Stroke more commonly causes focal neurological deficits.
n.2: Hypoglycaemia commonly causes sweating and confusion rather than tingling from overbreathing.
n.3: Anaphylaxis usually involves allergic signs such as rash or wheeze.
n.4: Airway obstruction would impair airflow rather than cause overbreathing.

Medical Emergencies.q: A conscious diabetic patient is shaky, confused and sweating. They are able to swallow safely. What is the best action?
o: Give fast-acting glucose and reassess response
Place them in the recovery position immediately
Give GTN spray under the tongue
Withhold all oral intake and continue observing
Medical Emergencies.w: A conscious patient with likely hypoglycaemia who can swallow should receive fast-acting glucose promptly.

n.1: Recovery position is for an unconscious breathing patient.
n.2: GTN is used for angina, not low blood glucose.
n.3: Delaying treatment may worsen hypoglycaemia.
n.4: CPR is not indicated in a conscious responsive patient.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient is hyperventilating, anxious and tingling in the fingers but remains responsive. What is the best immediate action?
o: Reassure, stop treatment and coach slow controlled breathing
Place the patient prone on the floor
Force the patient to breathe into a paper bag
Medical Emergencies.w: Supportive reassurance and slowing breathing are appropriate for hyperventilation once serious causes are excluded.

n.1: Adrenaline is not indicated for simple hyperventilation.
n.2: Prone positioning is unnecessary and unhelpful.
n.3: CPR is not indicated in a responsive patient.
n.4: Paper bag breathing is not recommended.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient treated for hypoglycaemia becomes alert and symptoms resolve. What is the best next step?
o: Monitor, provide longer-acting carbohydrate if appropriate, and reassess
Send the patient home alone at once
Give GTN spray to prevent relapse
Lay the patient flat for one hour regardless of condition
Medical Emergencies.w: After recovery, continued monitoring and follow-up carbohydrate intake may help maintain glucose levels.

n.1: Immediate treatment restart may be inappropriate.
n.2: Abrupt discharge without reassessment may be unsafe.
n.3: GTN has no role in hypoglycaemia management.
n.4: Positioning should reflect the patient's condition, not a fixed rule.

Medical Emergencies.q: During CPR, chest compressions are being delivered too slowly at around 60 per minute. Which interpretation is most accurate?
o: The rate is inadequate and should be increased
The rate is ideal if compressions are deeper
The rate is acceptable when two rescuers are present
The rate should be reduced further to avoid fatigue
The rate only matters once the AED arrives
Medical Emergencies.w: An adult compression rate of about 100–120 per minute is recommended, so 60 per minute is too slow.

n.1: Depth does not compensate for an inadequate compression rate.
n.2: Two rescuers do not change the target compression rate.
n.3: Reducing the rate further would worsen perfusion.
n.4: Effective compressions matter immediately, not only after AED arrival.

Medical Emergencies.q: Which feature best identifies airway obstruction in a conscious adult patient?
o: Unable to speak or cough effectively
Warm flushed skin with no distress
Medical Emergencies.w: Inability to speak or cough effectively suggests severe airway obstruction.

n.1: Toothache alone does not indicate choking.
n.2: No distress signs make airway obstruction unlikely.
n.3: Speaking normally suggests airway patency.
n.4: Headache alone does not indicate obstruction.

Medical Emergencies.q: After a shock is delivered, what sequence should follow next?
o: Resume CPR immediately and follow further AED prompts
Check the pulse for one full minute before touching the patient
Remove the pads and reassess breathing first
Sit the patient upright to improve recovery chances
Wait silently for the AED to restart by itself
Medical Emergencies.w: CPR should restart immediately after a shock unless the patient shows clear signs of recovery, following AED prompts.

n.1: Routine prolonged pulse checks delay essential CPR.
n.2: Pads should remain attached for further analysis.
n.3: An upright position is inappropriate after cardiac arrest.
n.4: Prompt CPR should not be delayed.

Medical Emergencies.q: Which management error regarding emergency drugs and equipment is most serious?
o: Not knowing where the emergency kit is stored
Training staff to locate the AED
Medical Emergencies.w: If staff cannot locate the emergency kit quickly, critical treatment may be dangerously delayed.

n.1: Routine expiry checks are good practice.
n.2: Replacing used stock is appropriate and necessary.
n.3: Checklists support readiness rather than create risk.
n.4: Training staff to find the AED improves emergency response.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient becomes unresponsive in the waiting area, is not breathing normally, and no pulse is detected. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Begin chest compressions and call for the AED
Place the patient in the recovery position
Give high-flow oxygen and observe for response
Check the pulse again for a full minute
Move the patient to the dental chair before acting
Medical Emergencies.w: When a patient is unresponsive, not breathing normally and has no pulse, CPR should start immediately while another team member retrieves the AED.

n.1: Recovery position is only appropriate for a breathing unconscious patient.
n.2: Oxygen may be helpful later, but delaying compressions reduces survival chances.
n.3: Pulse checks should be brief; prolonged reassessment delays CPR.
n.4: Moving the patient first wastes critical time unless the environment is unsafe.

Medical Emergencies.q: Which item is most important to bring first when responding to a collapsed patient elsewhere in the practice?
o: Emergency drugs kit and AED if available
Medical Emergencies.w: Emergency response equipment such as the AED and emergency kit should be prioritised.

n.1: Administrative items are not immediate priorities.
n.2: Routine dental instruments are not first-line emergency equipment.
n.3: These may help later but are not priorities.
n.4: Impression materials are unrelated.

Medical Emergencies.q: During CPR, the chest is not returning fully to its normal position between compressions. What is the error that should be corrected?
o: Leaning on the chest between compressions
Medical Emergencies.w: Leaning prevents full chest recoil, reducing venous return and CPR effectiveness.

n.1: Frequent changes can be managed well and do not specifically cause poor recoil.
n.2: Early AED use is beneficial, not the issue described.
n.3: Oxygen timing does not explain lack of recoil.
n.4: Counting aloud may help coordination and is not the error shown.

Medical Emergencies.q: In a crowded waiting room, the AED has advised a shock. Which scenario-based action is best?
o: Loudly instruct everyone to stand clear, visually confirm, then deliver the shock
Press shock immediately because voice prompts are enough warning
Ask one person to hold the patient still while shocking
Remove the pads to make space around the patient
Delay indefinitely until the waiting room is empty
Medical Emergencies.w: The rescuer should clearly warn others, visually confirm nobody is touching the patient, then deliver the shock promptly.

n.1: Visual confirmation is still required.
n.2: Nobody should be touching the patient during shock delivery.
n.3: Pads should remain attached for defibrillation.
n.4: Unnecessary delay reduces the chance of successful defibrillation.

Medical Emergencies.q: During treatment, a patient says their tongue feels swollen and their voice sounds hoarse shortly after taking medication. What is the best recognition?
o: Possible evolving anaphylaxis with airway involvement
Routine numbness from local anaesthetic only
Medical Emergencies.w: Tongue swelling and hoarse voice may indicate airway oedema in anaphylaxis.

n.1: Airway symptoms should not be dismissed as routine numbness.
n.2: Dehydration does not typically cause sudden tongue swelling.
n.3: Anxiety does not usually cause visible swelling or hoarseness.
n.4: Angina presents with chest symptoms rather than airway swelling.

Medical Emergencies.q: Which action best identifies correct management of a conscious choking patient with ineffective cough?
o: Treat as severe choking and begin appropriate choking protocol
Ask them to lie flat immediately
Encourage them to eat something soft
Medical Emergencies.w: An ineffective cough in a conscious patient suggests severe choking requiring prompt intervention.

n.1: Water may worsen obstruction.
n.2: Lying flat may worsen airway compromise.
n.3: Food is inappropriate.
n.4: Delay is unsafe.

Medical Emergencies.q: A conscious patient is clutching their throat, unable to speak and making silent efforts to breathe. What should be recognised first?
Medical Emergencies.w: Inability to speak with silent respiratory effort suggests severe choking.

n.1: Asthma usually produces wheeze rather than inability to speak from obstruction.
n.2: Panic does not usually prevent speech with silent airflow obstruction.
n.3: Hyperglycaemia does not present this way.
n.4: Angina causes chest discomfort rather than choking signs.

Medical Emergencies.q: After local anaesthetic, a patient reports ringing in the ears, metallic taste and becomes restless. Which emergency may need recognising?
Medical Emergencies.w: Tinnitus, metallic taste and agitation after injection may indicate local anaesthetic toxicity.

n.1: Hunger does not explain temporal association with injection and neurological symptoms.
n.2: Syncope recovery does not typically cause metallic taste.
n.3: Asthma causes respiratory symptoms.
n.4: Stroke is less typical with this specific post-injection pattern.

Medical Emergencies.q: During two-person CPR in the practice, compressions are effective but ventilation attempts are repeatedly failing because the chest is not rising. What scenario-based response is most appropriate?
o: Reopen the airway and attempt a better seal before the next breaths
Stop compressions until perfect ventilations are achieved
Remove the AED pads to improve access
Continue ineffective breaths without changing technique
Move the patient onto the dental chair immediately
Medical Emergencies.w: If the chest is not rising, airway position and mask seal should be corrected while minimising interruptions to compressions.

n.1: Compressions should continue with only brief pauses as needed.
n.2: AED pads should remain attached once applied.
n.3: Persisting with ineffective technique does not oxygenate the patient.
n.4: Unnecessary movement delays ongoing resuscitation.

Medical Emergencies.q: Which option correctly identifies the usual adult AED pad placement?
o: One pad upper right chest, one pad left side below the armpit
Both pads placed centrally over the sternum
One pad on each shoulder only
Both pads on the lower left chest wall together
One pad on the abdomen and one on the sternum
Medical Emergencies.w: Standard adult pad placement is upper right chest and left lateral chest below the armpit unless pads indicate otherwise.

n.1: Pads should be separated to allow current to pass through the heart.
n.2: Shoulders are not standard defibrillation pad sites.
n.3: Pads placed together on one side are ineffective.
n.4: Abdominal placement is not standard for AED use.

Medical Emergencies.q: Which management error during CPR is most serious?
o: Stopping compressions for long unnecessary pauses
Medical Emergencies.w: Long interruptions reduce circulation and worsen CPR effectiveness.

n.1: Counting aloud may improve coordination.
n.2: Changing rescuers can maintain quality compressions.
n.3: AED use is beneficial.
n.4: Early escalation is appropriate.

Medical Emergencies.q: During a seizure, which action is most appropriate?
o: Protect the patient from injury and do not restrain movements
Insert a mouth prop between the teeth
Hold the limbs firmly to stop jerking
Move the patient immediately to another room
Medical Emergencies.w: The priority during seizure activity is preventing injury while allowing the seizure to run its course.

n.1: Nothing should be placed in the mouth during a seizure.
n.2: Restraint can cause injury.
n.3: Oral fluids are unsafe during a seizure.
n.4: Moving the patient may increase injury risk.

Medical Emergencies.q: Which error in recognition is most concerning when assessing a collapsed patient?
o: Mistaking agonal gasps for normal breathing
Asking for the patient’s medical history
Moving instruments away from the chair
Checking whether the area is safe
Medical Emergencies.w: Agonal gasps can occur in cardiac arrest and must not be mistaken for normal breathing.

n.1: History may be useful if time and condition allow, but is not the key recognition error here.
n.2: Making the area safer is appropriate.
n.3: Calling for help early is good practice.
n.4: Scene safety assessment is appropriate.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A dentist asks for an instrument used specifically to compact amalgam into a cavity preparation. Which type is required?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A condenser is used to compact amalgam and reduce voids during placement.

n.1: A burnisher smooths and adapts material surfaces rather than condensing bulk amalgam.
n.2: A plastic filling instrument is more commonly associated with placing non-sticky restorative materials such as temporary dressings or some composites.
n.3: An excavator removes carious dentine.
n.4: A flat plastic spatula is primarily for mixing or carrying materials.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A dentist asks for the instrument used to carry triturated amalgam from the amalgam well to the prepared cavity. Which instrument type is required?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: An amalgam carrier transfers mixed amalgam from the amalgam well to the cavity in small increments.

n.1: A burnisher smooths and adapts restorative material surfaces rather than transporting amalgam.
n.2: A plastic filling instrument is not the standard instrument for carrying amalgam from the well.
n.3: College tweezers are mainly used to transfer small items such as cotton rolls.
n.4: A spoon excavator is used to remove soft carious dentine.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A dentist requests a material for lining a deep cavity under amalgam because fluoride release is desired. Which is most suitable?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Glass ionomer liner bonds chemically to tooth structure and releases fluoride.

n.1: Pattern resin is not used as a cavity liner.
n.2: Heavy-body silicone is an impression material.
n.3: ZOE may interfere with resin materials and is not chosen primarily for lining deep permanent cavities here.
n.4: Impression plaster is not restorative.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A nurse prepares a shade guide and curing light together for an anterior composite procedure. Which sequence is most appropriate?
o: Select shade first, then isolate and use the curing light during restoration placement
Use the curing light first, then select shade after dehydration
Isolate fully, etch, cure adhesive, then compare shades
Cure an empty matrix band, then select the nearest shade tab
Place the restoration completely, then choose the best pre-operative shade
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Shade selection should be completed before dehydration from isolation, while the curing light is used later during restoration placement.

n.1: Curing first and selecting shade after dehydration risks an inaccurate match.
n.2: Shade should not be delayed until after operative steps begin.
n.3: Curing an empty matrix band is irrelevant to shade selection.
n.4: Selecting shade after completion defeats the purpose of pre-operative matching.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The dentist asks for item 8 before trituration. What type of item is this?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 8 is an amalgam capsule containing pre-proportioned alloy and mercury for trituration.

n.1: Glass ionomer capsules differ in design and use.
n.2: A local anaesthetic cartridge is a glass cartridge for use in a syringe.
n.3: A composite compule is extruded through a dispenser and has a different nozzle design.
n.4: Polishing paste containers are not triturated before use.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A dentist requests a more accurate final impression for a crown preparation. Which material is generally most suitable?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Addition silicone offers excellent dimensional stability and fine detail reproduction for crown work.

n.1: Alginate is useful for study models but less accurate for crown finals.
n.2: Impression compound lacks fine detail for this use.
n.3: Modelling wax is not a definitive impression material.
n.4: Temporary filling material is unrelated.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A nurse places the shade guide after rubber dam isolation has been in place for several minutes. Why is this poor equipment use?
o: Tooth dehydration may make the shade appear lighter than normal
The shade tabs become chemically unstable under isolation
Rubber dam makes enamel permanently darker
The tabs cannot be disinfected once isolation starts
Shade matching should only be done after polishing
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Teeth can dehydrate during isolation, leading to a lighter appearance and less reliable shade selection.

n.1: The issue is tooth appearance, not chemical instability of the tabs.
n.2: Dehydration does not make enamel permanently darker.
n.3: Disinfection is not the reason this timing is poor.
n.4: Shade is usually selected before restoration placement and polishing.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A patient reports sensitivity when drinking cold water after placement of a metallic restoration. Which property of metals contributes most to this?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Metals conduct temperature changes efficiently, which can transmit cold stimuli to the tooth.

n.1: Low compressive strength is not the reason for thermal sensitivity.
n.2: High solubility is not a typical explanation here.
n.3: Polymerisation contraction applies to resin materials, not metallic restorations.
n.4: Fluoride release is unrelated to metallic restorations.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A dentist selects a material for a posterior core build-up because it must resist heavy biting forces. Which property is most important?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Materials used in load-bearing areas should have high compressive strength to resist occlusal forces.

n.1: Low thermal conductivity may improve comfort but is not the main requirement for resisting heavy forces.
n.2: Taste is not a key structural property for a core build-up material.
n.3: Translucency is mainly aesthetic rather than mechanical.
n.4: Colour fade is unrelated to functional strength.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: On the image, item 2 contains two pastes mixed through a dispensing tip. Which restorative material is most likely supplied this way?
o: Zinc phosphate luting cement powder and liquid
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Automix cartridges with mixing tips are commonly used for addition silicone materials.

n.1: Zinc phosphate is supplied as separate powder and liquid for slab mixing.
n.2: Glass ionomer may be hand-mixed or capsulated, not normally in automix cartridges.
n.3: Amalgam uses sealed capsules for trituration.
n.4: Alginate is powder mixed with water.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The dentist asks for item 11 in the image during placement of an anterior composite. What type of instrument is this?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 11 is a plastic composite instrument used for placing and contouring resin materials.

n.1: A sickle scaler is used for periodontal debridement, not composite placement.
n.2: A periosteal elevator is a surgical instrument used to reflect soft tissue.
n.3: An amalgam well is a container, not a hand instrument for contouring.
n.4: An excavator removes soft carious dentine and has a different working end.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 6 in the image is set out beside the bonding system. What is the safest assumption about its use?
o: It is likely a small bottle for dispensing bonding agent or primer
It is intended for storing unused alginate after mixing
It should be used to hold mixed amalgam temporarily
It is the correct container for sterilising burs chairside
It is designed for cooling zinc phosphate cement before placement
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Small opaque dropper bottles are commonly used for light-sensitive bonding agents or primers.

n.1: Mixed alginate is not stored in this type of bottle.
n.2: Amalgam is not kept in such a container.
n.3: Sterilisation is not carried out in this bottle.
n.4: Cooling cement occurs on a slab, not inside a dropper bottle.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 3 in the image is being prepared before posterior composite placement. Which instrument type is it?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 3 is a compule dispenser used to extrude composite from a single-dose compule in a controlled way.

n.1: A burnisher is used to smooth or adapt restorative materials rather than dispense composite from compules.
n.2: A Tofflemire retainer secures a matrix band around a tooth.
n.3: A straight probe is used for examination and detection, not for dispensing material.
n.4: An amalgam well is a small container for holding mixed amalgam.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 10 in the image is laid out before mixing a luting cement. How should this item be classified?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 10 is a glass slab used as a cool mixing surface for certain cements and pastes.

n.1: A dappen dish is a small container, usually circular and deeper.
n.2: An instrument cassette lid is part of a sterilisation container.
n.3: An occlusal registration plate is not used as a mixing surface.
n.4: A bur block is designed to hold rotary instruments.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The dentist requests the image item 12, then asks for protective orange shield positioning. Why is this necessary?
o: To reduce operator and patient exposure to curing light glare
To cool the composite during mixing
To sterilise the tip between layers instantly
To improve shade selection under blue light
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Orange shields filter intense blue curing light and reduce glare exposure.

n.1: The shield is not a cooling device.
n.2: Mercury evaporation is unrelated and unsafe.
n.3: It does not sterilise equipment.
n.4: Blue curing light is not for shade matching.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 11 in the image is selected during contouring of a Class IV composite. What is its most likely use?
o: To place and shape composite without sticking excessively
To carry amalgam from the capsule into the cavity
To adjust a matrix retainer spindle intraorally
To remove soft carious dentine by excavation only
To wedge interproximally before band placement
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A plastic composite instrument is used to place and contour composite material while minimising sticking and distortion.

n.1: An amalgam carrier is used for amalgam transfer.
n.2: Matrix retainer adjustment requires different equipment.
n.3: Excavation is performed with an excavator, not this instrument.
n.4: Interdental wedging is done with wedges, not a composite instrument.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 10 in the image is laid out before mixing zinc phosphate cement. What type of item is it?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 10 is a glass slab used as a cool mixing surface for certain dental cements and pastes.

n.1: A rubber mixing bowl is used more commonly for materials such as alginate.
n.2: A dappen dish is a small container for holding small amounts of liquid or material.
n.3: A sterilisation cassette stores instruments for processing and transport.
n.4: An acrylic denture flask is laboratory equipment used in denture processing.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 2 in the image is being prepared for use with a light-body impression material. What should be done before clinical use?
o: Express a small amount first to ensure even flow from both pastes
Place it immediately into the mouth before attaching the tip
Shake the cartridge vigorously after seating the tray
Remove the mixing tip once the material starts flowing
Cool the cartridge on the glass slab for several minutes
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Bleeding a small amount first helps confirm both base and catalyst are flowing correctly before the mixing tip is used.

n.1: The tip must be attached and the material prepared properly before intraoral use.
n.2: Shaking after tray seating is inappropriate and risks inaccuracy.
n.3: Removing the tip during use would disrupt mixing and waste material.
n.4: Cooling the cartridge on a slab is not the standard step here.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A nurse prepares item 5 from the image for the dentist. In restorative procedures, how is this equipment most appropriately used?
o: To place a controlled amount of etchant or flowable material precisely
To triturate powder and liquid cement thoroughly
To carry amalgam from the mixing area to the mouth
To cool a cement mix during spatulation
To punch holes in rubber dam material
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A fine syringe is commonly used to apply materials such as etchant gels or certain flowable materials accurately.

n.1: Mixing cements is not done in a syringe.
n.2: An amalgam carrier transfers amalgam; a fine syringe does not.
n.3: Cooling occurs on a slab, not in this device.
n.4: Rubber dam punches are separate instruments.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A nurse loads too little material into a stock tray and the dentist records show-through areas. What error has occurred?
o: Insufficient tray loading leading to inadequate coverage
Incorrect bur speed during cavity prep
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Underloaded trays can produce show-through and incomplete impression detail.

n.1: Composite shrinkage is unrelated to tray impressions.
n.2: Bur speed does not explain tray show-through.
n.3: Shade issues are unrelated.
n.4: Glass ionomer curing is irrelevant here.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 6 in the image would most likely contain which product used with impression procedures?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Small bottles commonly contain tray adhesive for elastomeric impressions.

n.1: Alginate powder is stored in tubs or sachets.
n.2: Plaster powder is not stored in dropper bottles.
n.3: Dental stone is supplied in larger containers.
n.4: Compound sticks are solid materials.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: During placement of a posterior composite, the dentist requests item 12 from the image. What is its primary function?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 12 is an LED curing light used to polymerise light-cured resin materials.

n.1: Impression compound is softened by heat, not by a curing light.
n.2: Amalgam is triturated mechanically in an amalgamator.
n.3: Condensation requires hand instruments.
n.4: Ultrasonic scalers remove deposits, unrelated to curing composite.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 5 in the image is most suitable for dispensing which material accurately in small quantities?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A syringe with fine tip is commonly used for controlled placement of etchant gel.

n.1: Alginate is bulk mixed and tray loaded.
n.2: Amalgam is capsulated and condensed.
n.3: Putty silicone is hand mixed or dispensed in bulk.
n.4: Compound sticks are heated and handled differently.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The image shows shade tabs at item 13. Which interpretation is most accurate for shade selection?
o: Shade should be selected before tooth dehydration occurs
Shade is best chosen after polishing the final restoration only
Shade is unaffected by ambient lighting
Shade tabs are only for denture acrylics
Posterior teeth never require shade matching
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Natural tooth shade is best assessed early, before dehydration lightens enamel.

n.1: Waiting until after placement defeats pre-operative matching.
n.2: Lighting conditions significantly influence shade perception.
n.3: Shade guides are widely used for restorative matching.
n.4: Posterior aesthetics can still matter.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 5 in the image is most suitable for placing which impression-related material accurately around a preparation?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A syringe is commonly used to place light-body wash around prepared margins.

n.1: Alginate is not syringed as a powder slurry.
n.2: Compound pellets are heat softened, not syringed.
n.3: Plaster is not placed this way intraorally.
n.4: Wax blocks are shaped manually.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 5 in the image is prepared before phosphoric acid etch is applied. Which type of instrument is item 5?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 5 is a dispensing syringe used to apply small amounts of material accurately, such as etching gel.

n.1: A condenser compacts amalgam rather than dispensing etch.
n.2: A local anaesthetic syringe delivers anaesthetic cartridges and needles.
n.3: A bone rongueur is a surgical instrument for trimming bone.
n.4: A wax knife is used to shape waxes, not dispense etching gel.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 1 in the image is selected before mixing alginate. How should this item be classified?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 1 is a stock impression tray used to carry and retain impression material during impression taking.

n.1: A rubber dam frame supports sheet dam material during isolation.
n.2: An articulating paper holder is used to hold occlusal marking strips.
n.3: A surgical retractor is used to hold tissue aside during surgical procedures.
n.4: A bur block is used to organise rotary instruments.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The dentist requests item 11 from the image while shaping a Class IV composite. What type of instrument is item 11?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 11 is a composite placement instrument used to carry, adapt and contour resin material during restoration placement.

n.1: A periodontal probe is used to measure periodontal pockets, not to contour composite.
n.2: An amalgam carrier transfers amalgam into a cavity rather than shaping composite.
n.3: An excavator removes soft carious dentine and is not intended for composite contouring.
n.4: A matrix retainer secures a matrix band around a tooth and is not a shaping instrument.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 3 in the image is most accurately classified as which instrument type?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 3 is a compule dispenser used to express composite from single-dose compules.

n.1: An amalgam condenser is a hand instrument used to compact amalgam into a cavity.
n.2: A local anaesthetic syringe has a distinct cartridge and aspirating design.
n.3: A matrix retainer secures a matrix band around a tooth.
n.4: An articulating paper holder is unrelated to dispensing composite.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Which instrument type is most appropriate for carving occlusal anatomy into a recently condensed amalgam restoration?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A carver is specifically designed to reproduce grooves, ridges and anatomical form in amalgam.

n.1: A condenser compacts material but does not shape fine anatomy.
n.2: A mixing spatula is for preparation of materials, not carving restorations.
n.3: A composite brush is used with resin materials rather than amalgam carving.
n.4: An excavator is intended for removal of soft dentine, not carving anatomy.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The impression tears on removal around deep undercuts. Which material property was most likely inadequate?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Low tear strength increases risk of tearing in thin sections and undercuts.

n.1: Radiopacity is not the relevant issue here.
n.2: Blue light opacity is unrelated.
n.3: Compressive strength is less relevant to tearing on removal.
n.4: Thermal conductivity does not explain tearing.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: An impression repeatedly tears when removed from deep undercuts. Which property of the material is most likely inadequate?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Low tear strength increases the risk of tearing in thin sections and around undercuts.

n.1: Opacity does not determine resistance to tearing.
n.2: Setting colour is unrelated to tearing during removal.
n.3: Specific gravity alone does not explain this clinical failure.
n.4: Taste stability is irrelevant.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 10 is chilled before use when mixing zinc oxide eugenol impression paste. Why?
o: To slow the setting reaction and extend working time
To sterilise the slab surface chemically
To increase final expansion of the paste
To darken the shade for visibility
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Cooling the slab helps slow the reaction and provides longer working time.

n.1: Cooling does not sterilise the slab.
n.2: Expansion is not the intended effect.
n.3: Tray retention depends on fit and adhesive, not slab temperature.
n.4: Shade change is irrelevant.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A glass ionomer liner is chosen beneath a restoration partly because it may help reduce future caries risk. Which property is responsible?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Glass ionomer materials are valued for fluoride release, which may contribute to caries prevention.

n.1: High solubility would generally be undesirable clinically.
n.2: Metallic lustre is not a property of glass ionomer or related to caries prevention.
n.3: Extreme flexibility is not the relevant benefit here.
n.4: Low density alone does not explain preventive benefit.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The curing light tip is not cleaned between patients, and composite residue remains attached. What is the main risk?
o: Debris may reduce light transmission and compromise curing effectiveness
The residue will increase the intensity of the blue light
It will prevent the need for barrier protection
The composite shade will automatically become darker
The bonding agent will no longer require air thinning
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Residue on the tip can interfere with light output and reduce curing effectiveness, in addition to infection control concerns.

n.1: Debris does not improve light intensity.
n.2: Barrier protection remains necessary according to protocol.
n.3: Composite shade is not changed this way.
n.4: Air thinning of bonding agent is unrelated to debris on the light tip.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A silicone impression cannot be poured immediately. Which property makes addition silicone advantageous here?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Addition silicone remains dimensionally stable longer than many alternatives.

n.1: Corrosion resistance is not the relevant property.
n.2: Self-etching is unrelated to impressions.
n.3: Fluoride release is associated with some restorative materials.
n.4: Expansion would reduce accuracy.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A Class II amalgam is being placed and the dentist requests the device that secures a band around the tooth. Which instrument type is this?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A matrix retainer holds the matrix band around the tooth to help form proximal walls and contours.

n.1: A burnisher smooths restorative surfaces rather than securing matrix bands.
n.2: A rubber dam punch is used to create holes in dam material.
n.3: An excavator removes carious dentine.
n.4: A composite gun dispenses composite from compules.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: After condensation of amalgam, the dentist requests an instrument to reproduce grooves and occlusal anatomy. Which type is needed?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A carver is used to shape restorative material and reproduce anatomical form.

n.1: A condenser compacts material but does not create detailed anatomy effectively.
n.2: A mixing spatula is intended for preparation of materials rather than carving restorations.
n.3: A mouth mirror aids vision and retraction but does not carve anatomy.
n.4: A probe is an examination instrument rather than a carving instrument.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A nurse notices saliva contamination after etching but before bonding. What is the best action?
o: Rinse, dry appropriately and re-etch according to protocol
Proceed with bonding as contamination is harmless
Place lining cement over the area
Dry with cotton and skip further steps
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Contamination can reduce bond strength; the surface should be reconditioned following protocol.

n.1: Saliva contamination can compromise adhesion.
n.2: Longer curing does not restore contaminated enamel surface.
n.3: A liner does not replace bonding steps.
n.4: Drying alone may be insufficient.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A luting cement is selected because it must form a very thin layer beneath a crown to allow complete seating. Which property is most relevant?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Low film thickness helps crowns seat fully and accurately during cementation.

n.1: Surface hardness may matter later but does not primarily determine seating.
n.2: Shade value is not the key requirement under a crown.
n.3: High elasticity is not the principal property sought here.
n.4: Colour change is unrelated to crown seating.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A temporary restoration fractures repeatedly in a large cavity. Which material property is most relevant when selecting an alternative temporary material?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: For repeated fracture, strength under occlusal load is a key consideration.

n.1: Radiopacity alone does not solve fracture risk.
n.2: Translucency is mainly aesthetic.
n.3: Taste is secondary to function.
n.4: Colour change does not address breakage.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 1 in the image is best described as which type of instrument?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 1 is a perforated stock tray used for carrying and retaining impression material.

n.1: A rubber dam frame supports dam material and has a different design.
n.2: An endodontic measuring block is used for file length reference.
n.3: A sectional matrix ring is used around teeth during restorative treatment.
n.4: An articulator is laboratory equipment for mounting models.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Which instrument type is most suitable for compacting amalgam firmly into a cavity preparation to reduce voids?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A condenser is used to compact amalgam into the cavity and improve adaptation.

n.1: A carver is used later to shape and refine occlusal anatomy.
n.2: An applicator brush is used for applying some liquids or resins, not condensing amalgam.
n.3: A matrix band is a supporting device for wall formation, not a condensing instrument.
n.4: A dappen dish is a container, not a hand instrument.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: During removal of soft infected dentine from a cavity floor, which instrument type is most appropriate?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: An excavator is designed to remove softened carious dentine from a cavity preparation.

n.1: A burnisher is used for smoothing or adapting restorative material surfaces.
n.2: A composite placement instrument is used for carrying and contouring resin material.
n.3: A shade guide is used for colour selection.
n.4: An impression tray carries impression material, not carious tissue.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Addition silicone impressions can often be poured later than alginate impressions. Which material property best explains this?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Addition silicone has good dimensional stability, allowing more flexibility before casting models.

n.1: Radiopacity is not the reason an impression can be poured later.
n.2: Electrical conductivity is irrelevant in this context.
n.3: High thermal expansion would reduce accuracy rather than improve storage time.
n.4: Surface roughness does not primarily determine delayed pouring suitability.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A composite restoration appears lighter after dehydration from prolonged rubber dam isolation. What is the best action before final shade judgement?
o: Rehydrate teeth and reassess shade later
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Dehydrated teeth look lighter; rehydration can alter apparent shade.

n.1: Immediate replacement may be unnecessary.
n.2: Curing time does not correct dehydration colour change.
n.3: Polishing will not predictably darken shade.
n.4: Re-etching does not address colour assessment.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Which instrument type is most appropriate for carrying freshly mixed amalgam from the well to the prepared cavity?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: An amalgam carrier transports amalgam from the mixing area to the cavity preparation.

n.1: A Ward's carver shapes anatomy after amalgam placement.
n.2: A mouth mirror is for vision, retraction and illumination.
n.3: A matrix band pusher is not the standard instrument for transferring amalgam.
n.4: An endodontic plugger is used in root canal obturation procedures.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: During finishing of a new amalgam restoration, the dentist requests an instrument to smooth the surface and improve marginal adaptation before carving. Which type is most suitable?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A burnisher is used to smooth amalgam and improve adaptation at margins before final carving.

n.1: An excavator removes soft carious tissue and is not used for smoothing amalgam.
n.2: A periosteal elevator is a surgical instrument.
n.3: A matrix retainer secures a matrix band, not smooths restorations.
n.4: A plastic instrument is not the primary instrument for burnishing amalgam.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A restorative material is chosen for an anterior tooth because it closely mimics natural enamel appearance. Which property is most relevant?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Aesthetic translucency helps a material blend with natural enamel and dentine appearance.

n.1: Electrical conductivity is unrelated to appearance.
n.2: Odour is not an aesthetic matching property.
n.3: Maximum opacity alone may make the result appear artificial.
n.4: Dissolution rate would be undesirable clinically.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The dentist reports recurrent voids in a mixed alginate impression. Which error is most likely?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Poor spatulation commonly traps air and leaves voids in alginate.

n.1: Water temperature mainly alters setting time.
n.2: A clean damp tray is not the primary cause of voids.
n.3: Perforated trays help retention rather than cause voids.
n.4: Closed storage is desirable.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: After curing a composite increment, the surface remains tacky. What is the best interpretation?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A superficial tacky oxygen-inhibited layer is expected and aids bonding between increments.

n.1: Composite does not melt in this context.
n.2: Etchant strength does not create this classic surface finding.
n.3: Matrix tension is unrelated.
n.4: Shade guide contamination is irrelevant.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: After removing an alginate impression, the nurse sees many small bubbles on the occlusal surfaces. What is the most likely error?
o: Air incorporated while loading the tray
Water was too cold during mixing
The impression was rinsed after removal
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Air trapped during loading often creates surface voids and bubbles.

n.1: Tray rigidity is not the common cause of surface bubbles.
n.2: Cold water slows set rather than causing bubbles directly.
n.3: Rinsing is appropriate and not the main cause.
n.4: Light closure does not usually produce multiple bubbles.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: On the image, item 6 would most commonly contain which restorative adjunct?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Small opaque dropper bottles commonly contain bonding agents or primers.

n.1: Alginate powder is stored in tubs or sachets.
n.2: Amalgam alloy is supplied in capsules.
n.3: Zinc phosphate powder is jar supplied.
n.4: Putty silicone is supplied in tubs or cartridges.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A composite restoration is placed in small increments rather than one bulk mass to help control which material property effect?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Incremental placement helps reduce stresses associated with polymerisation shrinkage and improves curing depth.

n.1: Radiopacity is determined by formulation, not increment size.
n.2: Tea staining is not the main reason for incremental placement.
n.3: Taste alteration is unrelated.
n.4: Magnetic attraction is irrelevant.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A stock tray is overloaded and excess impression material repeatedly causes gagging. What is the best action?
o: Select the correct tray and load an appropriate amount of material
Use the same tray but increase the amount to improve retention
Seat the tray more slowly to let the patient adapt
Keep the tray in place longer before fully seating
Choose a darker shade of impression material
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Correct tray selection and appropriate loading reduce overflow, improve comfort and still allow adequate recording.

n.1: Increasing the amount would likely worsen overflow and gagging.
n.2: Slower seating does not solve overloading.
n.3: Delaying seating is unlikely to improve the situation and may affect accuracy.
n.4: Shade is irrelevant to impression tray loading.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 5 in the image is being prepared before etching enamel. Which instrument type is it?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 5 is a dispensing syringe used for controlled placement of materials such as etchant gel.

n.1: An amalgam carrier transfers triturated amalgam into a cavity.
n.2: An aspirating syringe is for local anaesthetic administration.
n.3: An endodontic irrigating cannula is used for canal irrigation.
n.4: A three-in-one syringe delivers air and water from the dental unit.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A glass slab is not dried before cement mixing, and moisture remains on the surface. Why is this poor equipment preparation?
o: Extra moisture can alter the intended powder-liquid ratio and handling
It will improve the film thickness automatically
It makes the cement more radiopaque
It prevents the cement from adhering to the restoration
It guarantees a longer working time without affecting properties
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Residual moisture can change the mix consistency and affect the setting characteristics of moisture-sensitive cements.

n.1: Film thickness is not predictably improved by contamination with water.
n.2: Radiopacity is not determined by surface moisture.
n.3: Adhesion effects are not the primary issue described here.
n.4: Although handling may change, the properties are not reliably preserved.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A matrix band is being placed for a Class II amalgam restoration. Which sequence is correct?
o: Select band, place retainer, adapt band, insert wedge, tighten
Insert wedge, select shade, etch enamel, tighten retainer, burnish
Place retainer, remove band, wedge later, cure light, polish
Mix amalgam, wedge first, then choose band size
Apply bonding agent, then fit matrix band only
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: The band is selected and assembled, adapted around the tooth, wedged and tightened to establish contour/contact.

n.1: This includes unrelated composite steps and poor order.
n.2: Curing light use is irrelevant to amalgam and sequence is incorrect.
n.3: Material should not be mixed before proper matrix preparation.
n.4: Bonding agent is not part of routine amalgam matrix placement.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A Class II restoration is being prepared and the dentist asks for the device that secures a matrix band around the tooth. Which instrument type is needed?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A matrix retainer holds and tightens a matrix band around the tooth during restoration placement.

n.1: An amalgam well is a container used to hold mixed amalgam.
n.2: A dappen dish holds small amounts of liquid or paste.
n.3: An excavator is used to remove soft carious dentine.
n.4: A shade guide is used for colour matching.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: When item 12 is used, why should the orange shield be positioned correctly?
o: To reduce exposure to the intense blue curing light
To improve retention of the impression tray
To prevent the composite from becoming too cold
To increase the etching effect on enamel
To stop alginate setting too quickly
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: The orange shield helps protect eyes from the intense blue light emitted during curing.

n.1: Tray retention depends on fit and impression material handling, not the curing light shield.
n.2: The shield does not control composite temperature.
n.3: Etching is performed chemically, not by the shield.
n.4: Alginate setting is unrelated to the curing light shield.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A temporary restoration wears down rapidly within weeks. Which material property was most likely insufficient?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Poor abrasion resistance can lead to rapid wear under occlusal function.

n.1: Radiographic contrast does not determine wear rate.
n.2: Colour saturation is unrelated to functional durability.
n.3: Working time affects handling, not long-term wear directly.
n.4: Thermal expansion alone is not the main cause of rapid wear.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Which instrument type is most appropriate for smoothing the surface of a newly placed amalgam restoration before final carving?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A burnisher is used to smooth amalgam and improve marginal adaptation before carving is completed.

n.1: An excavator removes soft dentine and is not designed for smoothing amalgam.
n.2: A periodontal scaler removes calculus from teeth.
n.3: A matrix retainer supports a matrix band and does not smooth restorations.
n.4: A spatula is a mixing instrument rather than a finishing instrument.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 2 in the image is most commonly associated with which impression material system?
o: Zinc oxide eugenol paste for dressings only
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Cartridges with mixing tips are commonly used for automix addition silicone materials.

n.1: Impression plaster is not supplied in automix cartridges.
n.2: Alginate is mixed manually from powder and water.
n.3: This is not the usual format for dressings.
n.4: Compound sticks are heat softened.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Before seating an impression tray, item 1 in the image is tried in the mouth. What is the main reason for this?
o: To confirm fit, extension and patient comfort before loading material
To determine the final shade of the restoration
To check the curing depth of composite resin
To cool zinc phosphate cement during mixing
To establish occlusion after the restoration is placed
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A stock tray is tried in first to ensure correct size, extension and comfort before impression material is loaded.

n.1: Shade selection is performed with a shade guide, not an impression tray.
n.2: Curing depth is unrelated to tray try-in.
n.3: Cooling cement is not the purpose of tray selection.
n.4: Occlusion is not established with the stock tray.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The image shows item 10. During composite placement, how is this item most appropriately used?
o: As a mixing slab for small increments of materials
As a bite block during treatment
As a tray for sterilising burs
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Item 10 is a glass slab, commonly used as a cool mixing surface for some dental materials.

n.1: A bite block is designed differently and sits intraorally.
n.2: Glass slabs are not sterilising trays.
n.3: They are unrelated to suction devices.
n.4: A denture flask lid is unrelated laboratory equipment.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 10 in the image is prepared before mixing zinc phosphate cement. What is the correct use of this equipment?
o: To provide a cool glass surface that extends working time during mixing
To support the rubber dam during isolation
