To hold burs during sterilisation only
To block out undercuts before impression taking
To protect the patient from curing light glare
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A glass slab is used as a cool mixing surface for some cements, helping control the exothermic reaction and extend working time.

n.1: A rubber dam frame supports the dam, not a glass slab.
n.2: Burs are not stored on a mixing slab.
n.3: Undercut block-out is not the function of a glass slab.
n.4: Curing light protection is provided by a shield, not a slab.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 11 in the image would most likely be used for which task during restorative treatment?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A plastic composite instrument is used to place and contour resin materials.

n.1: Trituration is machine based.
n.2: Radiographs require holders/sensors.
n.3: Sharpening uses stones or devices.
n.4: Anaesthetic cartridges are unrelated.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The mixed alginate appears grainy with unmixed powder. What is the best interpretation?
o: The tray was too large only
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A grainy mix with visible particles usually indicates inadequate spatulation.

n.1: Tray adhesive does not create unmixed powder in alginate.
n.2: Disinfection occurs after impression removal.
n.3: Patient movement may distort shape, not cause powder lumps.
n.4: Tray size alone does not explain the mix texture.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: During composite placement, the curing light is held too far from the restoration. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Reduced light intensity at the material and incomplete curing
Faster polymerisation with less shrinkage stress
A stronger bond to dentine without adhesive
A smoother surface requiring no polishing
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Increasing the distance between the curing tip and the restoration can reduce the energy delivered and compromise curing.

n.1: Greater distance does not improve polymerisation quality.
n.2: An improved seal is not a predictable result of poor curing position.
n.3: Adhesive bonding is still required and not replaced by light position.
n.4: Surface quality and polishing requirements are not improved by holding the light too far away.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A temporary crown cemented with eugenol cement is to be replaced with a bonded composite restoration the same visit. What is the best action?
o: Remove residual eugenol thoroughly and use a non-eugenol temporary if needed
Leave the cement as it improves bonding
Etch directly over the eugenol residue only
Place amalgam instead of composite automatically
Delay treatment for exactly six months
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Eugenol can inhibit resin polymerisation, so residue should be removed and non-eugenol alternatives considered.

n.1: Residual eugenol may reduce resin bond strength.
n.2: Etching alone does not reliably remove contamination.
n.3: Material choice should be clinical, not automatic.
n.4: An arbitrary delay is unnecessary.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A newly mixed zinc phosphate cement becomes excessively warm on mixing. What is the best action next time?
o: Use a chilled glass slab and incorporate powder incrementally
Add water to cool the mix rapidly
Reduce spatulation to five seconds only
Use a paper pad instead of slab
Place it immediately before mixing is complete
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Zinc phosphate is exothermic; a cool slab and staged powder addition extend working time.

n.1: Adding water changes properties and is incorrect.
n.2: Insufficient mixing harms consistency.
n.3: Paper pads do not dissipate heat as effectively.
n.4: Incomplete mixing compromises cement.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 2 and its tip are used. Which sequence is correct for an automix silicone impression?
o: Bleed small amount, attach tip, load tray, syringe wash, seat tray
Seat tray first, then attach tip, then bleed cartridge
Mix by hand, remove tip, then seat empty tray
Load tray, disinfect, then add wash intraorally later
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: The cartridge is bled, tip attached, tray loaded, wash placed, then tray seated promptly.

n.1: The tray cannot be seated before material preparation.
n.2: Automix systems are not hand mixed in this manner.
n.3: Disinfection occurs after use, not before seating.
n.4: Delayed tip placement wastes working time.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The mixing tip on an automix impression cartridge is reused after the first impression has set inside it. What error has occurred?
o: A blocked or partially blocked tip may prevent correct mixing and extrusion
The material will become more dimensionally stable
The wash material will set more slowly and improve detail
The tray will require no adhesive
The impression will become easier to remove from undercuts
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Set material in the tip can obstruct flow and disrupt correct mixing of base and catalyst.

n.1: Reusing a blocked tip does not improve stability.
n.2: Setting behaviour is not improved by reusing the tip.
n.3: Tray adhesive requirements are unchanged.
n.4: Removal from undercuts is unrelated to a blocked tip.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: During amalgam placement, the mix appears dry and crumbly immediately after trituration. What is the best interpretation?
o: The amalgam is undertriturated or incorrectly proportioned
Condensation pressure was too high already
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Dry crumbly amalgam commonly indicates undertrituration or proportion issues.

n.1: Ideal amalgam should be workable and cohesive.
n.2: Excess mercury often gives a wetter appearance.
n.3: This is unrelated to polishing.
n.4: Condensation has not yet corrected the mix.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 10 in the image would be most useful during mixing of which material?
o: Zinc oxide eugenol impression paste on a slab
Impression compound in a water bath
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A glass slab is commonly used for mixing certain pastes such as zinc oxide eugenol systems.

n.1: Alginate is usually mixed in a flexible bowl.
n.2: Putty silicone is commonly hand mixed.
n.3: Compound is softened with heat rather than slab mixed.
n.4: Adhesive is painted on, not slab mixed.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A composite instrument is used dry and repeatedly drags the material out of the cavity. What is the best action?
o: Use the instrument appropriately and minimise sticking while maintaining material control
Switch immediately to an amalgam carrier for all composite placement
Increase etching time to stop the dragging
Use the curing light between every movement before adaptation
Change the shade guide before continuing placement
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Correct handling of the composite instrument aims to place and shape material without unnecessary dragging or distortion.

n.1: An amalgam carrier is not the correct placement instrument for composite.
n.2: Etching time does not address instrument drag during placement.
n.3: Curing between every movement would be impractical and may impair adaptation.
n.4: Shade guide use is unrelated to this handling issue.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: Item 1 in the image rocks during try-in before loading. What is the best action?
o: Select a better-fitting tray before mixing material
Add extra water to thin the mix
Use less material so rocking stops
Seat only on one side first
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Tray fit should be corrected before mixing to avoid distortion and poor extension.

n.1: Changing water ratio compromises material properties.
n.2: Proceeding with an unstable tray risks an inaccurate impression.
n.3: Reducing material does not correct tray fit.
n.4: Uneven seating may worsen distortion.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A restorative material expands and contracts at a rate close to natural tooth structure. Why is this advantageous?
o: It may reduce marginal gap formation with temperature changes
It eliminates the need for bonding agents
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A thermal expansion coefficient similar to tooth tissue may help maintain marginal integrity during temperature changes.

n.1: Plaque accumulation depends on multiple factors, not thermal expansion alone.
n.2: Bonding requirements are not eliminated by matching expansion rates.
n.3: Sensitivity can have many causes and is not fully prevented by this property.
n.4: Shade stability is a separate material characteristic.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: An alginate impression sets before the tray is seated fully. What is the most likely cause?
o: Water temperature was too warm during mixing
The tray adhesive was left to dry
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Warm water accelerates the chemical reaction and shortens alginate working time.

n.1: Tray adhesive is not routinely the cause of premature alginate set.
n.2: Perforations help retention and do not speed setting.
n.3: Bowl type is less significant than water temperature.
n.4: Patient rinsing does not cause rapid setting.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: For posterior composite placement, which instrument type is most suitable for applying and contouring successive increments without dragging the material excessively?
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A composite placement instrument is designed for carrying, adapting and contouring resin increments.

n.1: A sickle scaler is a periodontal instrument.
n.2: A bone file is a surgical instrument for smoothing bone.
n.3: A cement spatula is used for mixing materials.
n.4: An aspirating syringe is used for local anaesthetic administration.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A mixed glass ionomer appears dull, grainy and sets before placement. What is the most likely cause?
o: Incorrect powder-to-liquid ratio with delayed mixing
Use of matrix band before mixing
Excess moisture contamination after final set only
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Too much powder or delayed incorporation shortens working time and creates a grainy mix.

n.1: Matrix placement does not cause premature set of the material.
n.2: Moisture contamination affects surface integrity, not the initial grainy mix.
n.3: Shade selection does not change handling in this way.
n.4: A clean spatula is appropriate and not causative.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: A posterior composite is being placed in 2 mm increments rather than one bulk mass. What is the best interpretation?
o: Incremental placement improves curing depth and reduces shrinkage stress
It is only done to change tooth shade
It prevents the need for bonding agent
It is required only for amalgam restorations
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Incremental placement helps light penetration and limits polymerisation stress.

n.1: Shade effects are secondary, not the main reason.
n.2: Bonding is still required.
n.3: Finishing and polishing may still be necessary.
n.4: This rationale applies to composite, not amalgam.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: During an impression procedure, the selected stock tray leaves inadequate coverage of the molar area. What is the best interpretation of this equipment problem?
o: The tray is incorrectly sized and may produce an incomplete impression
The alginate has been mixed for too long only
The patient has closed too firmly on the tray
The tray is too rigid for any impression material
The impression material must be light-cured instead
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: A tray that does not adequately cover the intended area is poorly selected and may fail to capture required detail.

n.1: Mixing time may affect set, but not the tray's area coverage.
n.2: Patient closure does not explain inadequate extension of the tray.
n.3: Rigidity itself is not the core problem described.
n.4: Impression materials are not light-cured in this context.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: The image shows item 7. In restorative procedures this would most commonly be used to:
o: Apply or dispense small amounts of bonding liquid
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Small dispenser bottles are commonly used for primers or bonding liquids.

n.1: Carving requires metal hand instruments.
n.2: Retainers are tightened mechanically.
n.3: Heating endodontic materials is unrelated.
n.4: Vertical dimension is a prosthodontic measurement task.

Dental Materials & Equipment.q: What is the best action immediately after removing an impression from the mouth?
o: Rinse, inspect and disinfect according to protocol
Leave it dry on the bracket table
Pour stone before rinsing blood or saliva
Store in direct sunlight to harden
Dental Materials & Equipment.w: Impressions should be rinsed, checked and disinfected promptly using local protocol.

n.1: Leaving contamination on the impression is poor practice.
n.2: Trimming is not the immediate priority.
n.3: Rinsing and disinfection should occur first.
n.4: Sunlight may distort some materials.

Clinical Procedures.q: The isolated tooth shown with the blue sheet and clamp arrangement is being managed with which technique?
Clinical Procedures.w: The blue sheet and clamp arrangement indicate rubber dam isolation, which provides moisture control and improved access during restorative treatment.

n.0: Cotton rolls do not produce the sealed field and clamp-retained sheet shown in the image.
n.2: High-volume suction helps with fluid control but does not create this form of tooth isolation.
n.3: Cheek retraction improves access but does not isolate an individual tooth in this way.
n.4: Dry guards may absorb moisture but do not resemble the clamped sheet shown.

Clinical Procedures.q: A patient says their new lower denture lifts during speech. What is the best next step?
Clinical Procedures.w: Clinical review is needed to assess stability, fit and adaptation.

n.1: Glue is inappropriate and may damage the denture.
n.2: Cleaning remains essential.
n.3: Immediate disposal is unnecessary.
n.4: Patients should not self-adjust dentures.

Clinical Procedures.q: The instruments placed into the isolated tooth most strongly indicate which stage of treatment is taking place?
Clinical Procedures.w: The presence of intracanal instruments within an isolated tooth indicates canal instrumentation during root canal treatment.

n.1: Final polishing would involve finishing instruments rather than files placed into the canals.
n.2: Impression taking does not involve intracanal instruments in an isolated tooth.
n.3: Occlusal adjustment is carried out after restoration placement and would not appear like this.
n.4: Matrix adaptation is a restorative procedure unrelated to the intracanal instruments shown.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which numbered item shows matrix bands and wooden wedges ready for proximal restoration placement?
Clinical Procedures.w: Item 6 contains matrix bands/clamps and wedges commonly used to rebuild proximal walls and contour restorations.

n.0: Item 1 contains general restorative items rather than matrix components.
n.1: Item 2 contains examination instruments only.
n.2: Item 4 contains suction aspirator tips.
n.3: Item 5 is the rubber dam punch.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which numbered item is the apex locator used during endodontic treatment to help determine canal working length electronically?
Clinical Procedures.w: Item 3 is the apex locator, the electronic device used to assist with working length determination during root canal treatment.

n.0: Item 1 is a tray of endodontic materials and consumables, not the electronic measuring device.
n.1: Item 2 is the operating microscope, which improves visibility rather than measuring canal length electronically.
n.3: Item 4 is the rubber dam and clamp used for isolation, not working length determination.
n.4: Item 5 contains files and obturation-related accessories rather than the apex locator unit.

Clinical Procedures.q: A patient feels faint immediately after extraction. What is the best immediate action?
Clinical Procedures.w: Reclining the chair and reassuring the patient helps manage a vasovagal episode.

n.1: The patient should remain supervised clinically.
n.2: Hot drinks are not immediate management.
n.3: Standing may worsen faintness.
n.4: Dismissal is unsafe while symptomatic.

Clinical Procedures.q: A patient asks why teeth feel smoother after treatment. What is the best explanation?
Clinical Procedures.w: Scaling removes rough deposits, leaving cleaner smoother surfaces.

n.1: Enamel is not replaced during periodontal treatment.
n.2: Roots are not shortened routinely.
n.3: Contacts are not widened for this reason.
n.4: Crowns were not necessarily involved.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which numbered item would most likely be selected when the operator asks for files and obturation-related accessories during canal preparation?
Clinical Procedures.w: Item 5 contains endodontic files and related accessories used during instrumentation and obturation stages.

n.0: Item 1 contains tray materials but is not the main collection of files shown separately.
n.1: Item 2 is the operating microscope.
n.2: Item 3 is the apex locator.
n.4: Item 6 shows the tooth in treatment rather than the instrument set itself.

Clinical Procedures.q: The tooth shown with clamp and blue sheet has been isolated mainly to achieve which outcome?
Clinical Procedures.w: Rubber dam provides improved moisture control, soft tissue retraction and clearer operating access.

n.0: Isolation is not intended to increase bleeding.
n.2: It does not whiten teeth.
n.3: It does not automatically shorten curing time.
n.4: Local anaesthetic decisions are separate from dam placement.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which numbered item is the instrument used to punch holes into a rubber dam sheet before placement?
Clinical Procedures.w: Item 5 is the rubber dam punch, identified by its plier-style handles and punching mechanism for creating holes in the dam sheet.

n.0: Item 1 shows a tray of restorative items rather than the hole-punching instrument itself.
n.1: Item 2 contains examination instruments, not the device used to prepare the rubber dam sheet.
n.2: Item 4 shows suction tips used for moisture control rather than dam preparation.
n.4: Item 6 includes matrix-related accessories and wedges, not the punch.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which numbered item includes matrix bands or associated accessories used to help restore a proximal surface accurately?
Clinical Procedures.w: Item 6 shows matrix-related components and wedges used to support contour and contact during restorative procedures.

n.0: Item 1 is a general tray setup and does not specifically identify the matrix accessories shown separately.
n.1: Item 2 contains a mouth mirror and hand instruments rather than matrixing aids.
n.2: Item 4 contains aspirator tips used for evacuation, not matrix support.
n.3: Item 5 is the rubber dam punch, which prepares the dam rather than supporting proximal contour.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which numbered item is most directly associated with maintaining asepsis of a single tooth during root canal treatment?
Clinical Procedures.w: Item 4 is the rubber dam and clamp set, which is essential for isolation and reduction of contamination during endodontic treatment.

n.0: The microscope improves visibility but does not itself isolate the tooth.
n.1: The apex locator measures canal length rather than maintaining asepsis.
n.3: Files prepare the canals but do not provide isolation.
n.4: Item 6 shows treatment in progress but the specific isolation device is item 4.

Clinical Procedures.q: A patient complains of a sore spot under a new denture. Best advice?
Clinical Procedures.w: A review appointment allows the clinician to identify and adjust pressure areas safely.

n.1: Home filing can damage the denture and tissues.
n.2: Cleaning should continue.
n.3: Glue should not be used as lining.
n.4: Sleeping in dentures is often discouraged.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which numbered item would most directly help maintain a dry working field by removing saliva during a restorative procedure?
Clinical Procedures.w: Item 4 shows suction tips used to remove saliva and fluid from the oral cavity during treatment.

n.0: Item 1 is a mixed tray arrangement rather than the suction device itself.
n.1: Item 2 contains examination instruments rather than equipment for evacuation.
n.3: Item 5 is a rubber dam punch and is not used to aspirate saliva.
n.4: Item 6 contains matrix accessories rather than suction equipment.

Clinical Procedures.q: A patient reports a loose upper denture when speaking. What is the best next action?
Clinical Procedures.w: A clinical review is needed to assess fit, retention and required adjustments.

n.1: Household glue is unsafe and inappropriate.
n.2: Constant wear does not correct looseness.
n.3: Discarding it without assessment is unnecessary.
n.4: Patients should not trim dentures themselves.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which numbered item is most likely to be passed when the operator requests a mouth mirror during restoration placement?
Clinical Procedures.w: Item 2 includes the mouth mirror used for indirect vision, retraction and illumination.

n.0: Item 1 is a tray setup rather than the numbered mirror set requested.
n.2: Item 4 contains aspirator tips.
n.3: Item 5 is the dam punch.
n.4: Item 6 contains matrix accessories.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which numbered item is the operating microscope used to improve visualisation of the pulp chamber and canal anatomy?
Clinical Procedures.w: Item 2 is the operating microscope, used to enhance magnification and illumination during endodontic procedures.

n.0: Item 1 is a tray of materials rather than a magnification device.
n.2: Item 3 is the apex locator, which assists with working length rather than magnification.
n.3: Item 5 contains endodontic instruments and accessories but is not the microscope.
n.4: Item 6 shows the tooth under treatment rather than the microscope itself.

Clinical Procedures.q: A patient continues to spit repeatedly after extraction. Why should this be discouraged?
Clinical Procedures.w: Repeated spitting can disturb the clot and delay healing.

n.1: Healing is not harmed by being too quick.
n.2: Spitting does not weaken anaesthetic.
n.3: It does not cause enamel wear directly.
n.4: Roots are unaffected.

Clinical Procedures.q: The image shows deposits on the lingual surfaces of lower incisors. What is the most likely interpretation?
Clinical Procedures.w: Lower anterior lingual surfaces commonly collect calculus due to salivary duct proximity.

n.1: Fracture lines do not appear as tenacious deposits.
n.2: Bridge failure would be localised to an abutment tooth.
n.3: Gel residue would not resemble mineralised deposits.
n.4: Orthodontic cement excess has a different appearance.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which numbered item shows the materials most likely to include irrigants and endodontic consumables used chairside during treatment?
Clinical Procedures.w: Item 1 shows a tray containing consumables and solutions likely used for endodontic procedures, including irrigants and accessory items.

n.1: Item 2 is the operating microscope, which assists vision rather than supplying irrigants.
n.2: Item 3 is an apex locator.
n.3: Item 4 is rubber dam isolation equipment.
n.4: Item 5 is mainly the file and accessory set rather than the tray of liquids and consumables.

Clinical Procedures.q: The instruments shown within the isolated tooth indicate which stage of treatment is most likely taking place?
o: Final polishing of a composite restoration
Root canal instrumentation within the canals
Crown preparation for an indirect restoration
Placement of a matrix band for a Class II cavity
Clinical Procedures.w: The isolated tooth with endodontic files placed into the canals indicates instrumentation during root canal treatment.

n.0: Polishing would not involve files placed into root canals.
n.2: Crown preparation uses rotary preparation instruments rather than canal files in this arrangement.
n.3: Periodontal charting does not involve intracanal instruments.
n.4: Matrix band placement is a restorative procedure unrelated to the canal instruments shown.

Clinical Procedures.q: A patient asks why they must bite on gauze after extraction. Best explanation?
Clinical Procedures.w: Firm pressure on gauze helps stabilise a blood clot in the socket.

n.1: Gauze does not prevent enamel cracks.
n.2: It should not loosen teeth.
n.3: It does not numb the tongue.
n.4: Healing still takes time.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which numbered item would most likely be selected when the operator asks for a saliva ejector tip?
Clinical Procedures.w: Item 4 shows aspirator tips used to remove saliva and fluids during treatment.

n.0: Item 1 is a mixed tray setup rather than the suction tip requested.
n.1: Item 2 contains examination instruments.
n.3: Item 5 is a rubber dam punch.

Clinical Procedures.q: After access has been gained in non-surgical root canal treatment, which sequence is most appropriate?

Shaping, final restoration, drying, working length confirmation

Clinical Procedures.q: The operator asks for composite to be placed in several small increments rather than one large bulk. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The operator wants the final restoration to appear more translucent
Incremental placement is being used to improve curing and limit shrinkage stress
The cavity preparation is unsuitable for bonding agents
This method is mainly to avoid the need for any finishing or polishing
The aim is to reduce the number of instruments required chairside

n.0: Appearance can be influenced by layering, but the primary reason here is material performance rather than translucency alone.
n.2: Incremental placement does not indicate that bonding agents are unsuitable.
n.3: Finishing and polishing may still be required after incremental placement.
n.4: Instrument count is not the main reason for choosing an incremental technique.

Clinical Procedures.q: While assisting with placement of a matrix band for a Class II restoration, the patient closes suddenly with instruments in place. What is the best action?
o: Ask the patient to remain still and continue immediately
Withdraw instruments safely and check for injury before proceeding
Tighten the matrix band quickly before the patient moves again
Use suction to improve visibility and continue the procedure
Place the restorative material without further delay

n.2: Attempting to complete a step quickly in an unsafe moment could worsen injury.
n.3: Improved visibility does not address the immediate need to protect the patient.
n.4: Material placement should not continue until safety has been restored and any trauma assessed.

Clinical Procedures.q: A mixing pad has been contaminated by spray before glass ionomer is prepared. What is the best action?
o: Use the damp area because liquid is already present
Replace the pad and prepare a clean mixing surface
Use only material from the centre of the pad

n.0: Unknown moisture content can compromise the mix.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which material is commonly used to etch enamel before placing a bonded composite restoration?

Clinical Procedures.q: During root surface debridement, visibility becomes poor due to mist. What is the best action by the nurse?

n.1: Reducing lighting worsens visibility.

Clinical Procedures.q: Paper points inserted after irrigation are still emerging noticeably wet. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The canal may not yet be dry enough for obturation
The master cone fit has been confirmed
The access cavity outline is ideal
The canal has definitely been over-instrumented
The temporary restoration can now be placed
Clinical Procedures.w: Persistently wet paper points suggest that the canal may still contain moisture and may not yet be ready for obturation.

n.1: Paper point wetness does not confirm the fit of the master cone.
n.2: Access cavity design is not determined by whether paper points emerge wet.
n.3: Moist paper points alone do not prove over-instrumentation.
n.4: Moisture control within the canal is a separate issue from placing a temporary restoration.

Clinical Procedures.q: During etching for an anterior composite restoration, the nurse notices saliva contamination on the prepared tooth before bonding. What is the best action?
o: Proceed with bonding to avoid overdrying the tooth
Inform the operator immediately so the surface can be managed appropriately
Dry the area forcefully for longer and continue without mentioning it
Place the first composite increment quickly before more moisture appears
Apply additional etchant without informing the operator
Clinical Procedures.w: Saliva contamination can compromise bonding, so the operator should be informed immediately so the surface can be re-managed appropriately.

n.0: Proceeding without correcting contamination risks reduced bond effectiveness and restoration failure.
n.2: Forceful drying alone does not reliably correct contamination and may introduce further problems.
n.3: Composite should not be placed onto a surface that may be compromised.
n.4: Re-etching may or may not be required, but it should not be done unilaterally without informing the operator.

Clinical Procedures.q: Paper points placed in a canal are repeatedly coming out heavily wet after irrigation. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The master cone fit is already confirmed
The canal may not yet be sufficiently dried for obturation
Working length has definitely been lost
The access cavity is too small for instrumentation
The file sequence has been completed incorrectly
Clinical Procedures.w: Persistently wet paper points suggest the canal is not yet sufficiently dry, which may mean obturation should not proceed at that stage.

n.0: Moisture on paper points does not confirm master cone fit.
n.2: Wet paper points alone do not prove that working length has been lost.
n.3: Access size may affect handling, but repeated wetness mainly indicates moisture within the canal.
n.4: File sequence issues are not the most direct interpretation of persistently wet paper points.

Clinical Procedures.q: A temporary crown cement dislodges soon after seating and appears watery. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The mix ratio may have been incorrect
The crown margin was polished too much
Clinical Procedures.w: A thin watery mix may reduce retention and indicate incorrect powder-liquid proportioning.

n.0: Ideal occlusion does not explain weak cement.
n.2: Polishing margins is not the likely cause.
n.3: Isolation does not make cement watery.
n.4: Shade is irrelevant to retention.

Clinical Procedures.q: After placement of a temporary dressing, the patient says the tooth feels high on biting. What is the best action?
o: Advise the patient it will settle naturally
Ask the operator to check occlusion before dismissal
Tell the patient to avoid chewing for a week
Clinical Procedures.w: A high restoration should be assessed and adjusted by the operator before the patient leaves.

n.3: Avoiding chewing does not correct occlusal discrepancy.

Clinical Procedures.q: Two days after a deep posterior restoration, the patient reports sensitivity on biting. Which interpretation is most appropriate to relay to the operator?
o: The symptoms confirm that extraction is now required
The restoration may need review for occlusion, pulpal response or marginal seal
The complaint proves the local anaesthetic has not fully worn off
This finding means the matrix band used was too wide
The patient should simply avoid chewing on that side for several months
Clinical Procedures.w: Post-operative biting sensitivity can have several causes, including high occlusion, pulpal irritation or marginal issues, so a clinical review is appropriate.

n.0: Sensitivity alone does not confirm that extraction is necessary.
n.2: Two days later, persistent biting sensitivity is unlikely to be explained solely by residual anaesthetic.
n.3: Matrix width alone does not adequately explain the range of causes for post-operative biting sensitivity.
n.4: Avoidance without review risks missing a problem that may need correction.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which instrument is specifically designed to compact amalgam into a cavity preparation during placement?

n.2: An excavator is mainly used to remove soft carious tissue or debris.
n.3: A plastic instrument is commonly used for handling restorative materials such as composite, not condensing amalgam.
n.4: A scaler is used for periodontal instrumentation rather than restorative condensation.

Clinical Procedures.q: A file is dropped onto a non-sterile surface during preparation of the second canal. What is the best action?
o: Rinse it in irrigant and continue
Replace it with a sterile file of the same size and type
Wipe it with alcohol and use it for the coronal third only
Return it to use if it has not visibly soiled
Put it aside and use it later if needed

n.0: Irrigant is not a substitute for sterile instrument handling.
n.2: Wiping or limiting use does not restore sterility.
n.3: Lack of visible debris does not mean the file is suitable for reuse chairside.
n.4: A contaminated file should not be held for later clinical use.

Clinical Procedures.q: Which material is most commonly supplied as a phosphoric acid gel for enamel etching before composite bonding?

n.4: Petroleum jelly is not an etchant.

Clinical Procedures.q: While fitting a matrix system, the band keeps lifting away from the gingival margin as the retainer is tightened. What is the most likely interpretation?

Clinical Procedures.q: A temporary crown becomes loose shortly after cementation, and the cement mix had appeared very runny at the time of use. What is the most likely interpretation?

The patient's bite was definitely balanced correctly
The impression material used earlier was hydrophobic
The polishing stage was carried out too late

n.4: Polishing timing is not the likely reason for early loss of a crown with a visibly runny cement mix.

Clinical Procedures.q: During irrigation, sodium hypochlorite is accidentally drawn up into an unlabelled syringe on the tray. What is the best action?

Dilute the solution with water and continue to use it
Pass it only for canal lubrication rather than irrigation

n.3: Dilution does not resolve the problem of unsafe identification and may alter the intended concentration.

n.4: Fluoride varnish is unrelated.

Clinical Procedures.q: After extraction, the patient asks when to remove the gauze pack. Best advice is usually to:

n.4: Shade opacity can influence curing depth in some cases, but the direct interpretation here is inadequate curing rather than a finishing issue.

n.4: Torque drivers are associated with implants.

n.2: Scaling packs include periodontal instruments.

Clinical Procedures.q: A syringe of irrigant is passed without the side-vented needle requested by the operator. What error is most likely if this goes unnoticed?

Improved contact point formation in the proximal box
More accurate shade matching under the operating light

Clinical Procedures.q: Which item is most appropriate for grasping and removing a tooth crown during routine extraction?

Clinical Procedures.q: During canal irrigation, the nurse notices that sodium hypochlorite has been drawn into an unlabelled syringe. What is the best action?

Discard it safely and replace it with a correctly identified syringe
Use it only for the first canal instrument pass
Dilute it with water so it becomes less hazardous
Pass it immediately before there is any confusion

Clinical Procedures.q: A matrix band is removed before the restorative material has adequately set. What error is most likely?

Clinical Procedures.q: Which material is commonly used to etch enamel before placement of a bonded composite restoration?

n.4: Petroleum jelly is not used to create the etched enamel surface required for bonding.

Clinical Procedures.q: The apex locator display repeatedly gives unstable readings while the file is in the canal. What is the most likely interpretation?

Inform the operator immediately so isolation can be re-established
Use high-volume suction only and continue treatment
Dry the area repeatedly with cotton pellets and proceed
Delay mentioning it until the canal has been dressed

n.2: Suction helps control fluid but does not replace the seal provided by the rubber dam.
n.3: Repeated drying is not an adequate substitute for proper isolation.
n.4: Delay increases the risk of procedural compromise and contamination.

Clinical Procedures.q: A patient reports sensitivity to cold two days after a deep restoration. Which explanation is most appropriate to relay to the operator?

It is caused only by local anaesthetic
It can be ignored for several months

n.0: Sensitivity alone does not prove failure.
n.2: Extraction is not automatically indicated.
n.3: Local anaesthetic is not the sole explanation days later.
n.4: Persistent symptoms should not be ignored.

Clinical Procedures.q: Using the image, what is the most likely cause of the rough ledge retaining plaque?

n.1: A sound contour would not create a ledge.

n.3: Polished surfaces are smoother, not plaque retentive.
n.4: A clean margin should not appear as a rough ledge.

Clinical Procedures.q: During crown cementation, the prepared tooth becomes repeatedly contaminated with saliva just before seating. What is the best action?
o: Seat the crown quickly before the cement starts to set

Use only floss instead of brushing
